concept.definition: An equation carries the equality sign and an expression does not, so 5x and 2x - 3 are expressions while 5x = 25 and 2x - 3 = 9 are equations.

knowledge_items.statement: The presence of an equality sign is the one mark that turns an expression such as 5x into an equation such as 5x = 25.

abilities.ability: Sort a written item into expression or equation
abilities.description: Look for an equality sign and decide whether what is written is an expression or an equation.

ability_refs: Sort a written item into expression or equation

competencies.statement: Tells apart the two kinds of algebraic statement before deciding what may be done with them.
ability_refs: Sort a written item into expression or equation

misconceptions.statement: Learners try to find the value of x in 2x - 3 as though the expression were an equation waiting to be solved.
misconceptions.root_cause: Both expressions and equations use letters, so the absence of the equality sign goes unnoticed.
misconceptions.correction: Ask what the expression is supposed to equal, and show there is nothing to set it against.

real_world_applications.example: A spreadsheet treats a typed formula and a typed comparison test as two different kinds of entry.

pedagogy_recommendations.why_effective: Rapid sorting of cards marked expression or equation fixes the distinction before any solving begins.

learning_objectives.objective: Classify given algebraic items such as 5x and 5x = 25 as expressions or equations.

learning_outcomes.outcome: Separates a list of algebraic items into expressions and equations using the equality sign.

assessment_blueprint.recommended_question: Which of 2x - 3 and 2x - 3 = 9 is an equation, and what single mark decides it?
Write one expression and one equation of your own, and explain what distinguishes the two.

concept.definition: The expression written to the left of the equality sign is the LHS and the one to its right is the RHS, and naming them is what makes the balancing method describable.

knowledge_items.statement: An equation has two sides, the expression left of the equality sign and the one right of it, called the LHS and the RHS.

abilities.ability: Name the two sides of a given equation
abilities.description: Point out which expression is the LHS and which is the RHS in an equation such as 2x - 3 = 9.

skills.skill: Describing an equation in words before working on it
ability_refs: Name the two sides of a given equation

competencies.statement: Describes the parts of an equation precisely enough to explain each solving step aloud.
ability_refs: Name the two sides of a given equation
skill_refs: Describing an equation in words before working on it

misconceptions.misconception: The answer always sits on the right
misconceptions.statement: Learners expect the RHS to hold the answer and the LHS to hold the working that led to it.
misconceptions.root_cause: Arithmetic is written with the result after the equality sign, so that habit is carried into algebra.
misconceptions.correction: Show equations such as 9 = 2x - 3 where the bare number stands on the left instead.

real_world_applications.example: An accountant balancing a ledger names the two columns before explaining which entry was moved.

pedagogy_recommendations.why_effective: Setting equations on a two pan balance puts the naming of each side into the learner's own hands.

learning_objectives.objective: Label the LHS and the RHS of a given linear equation.

learning_outcomes.outcome: Identifies the left-hand side and the right-hand side of any equation presented to them.

assessment_blueprint.recommended_question: In the equation 2x - 3 = 9, which expression is the LHS?
Explain why the two sides must be named before the balancing method can be described at all.

concept.definition: The two expressions in an equation take equal values only for certain values of the variable, and those particular values are the solutions of the equation.

knowledge_items.statement: A solution of an equation is a value of the variable that makes the LHS and the RHS take the same value.

abilities.ability: Decide whether a value solves an equation
abilities.description: Put a proposed value into both sides and see whether the two results agree.

skills.skill: Treating an equation as a question about values
ability_refs: Decide whether a value solves an equation

competencies.statement: Understands solving as finding the values that make an equation true, not as shuffling symbols.
ability_refs: Decide whether a value solves an equation
skill_refs: Treating an equation as a question about values

misconceptions.misconception: Any value at all can be put in
misconceptions.statement: Learners think the variable in an equation stands for any number rather than for the values that make it true.
misconceptions.root_cause: In an expression the variable really can take any value, and that freedom is carried into equations.
misconceptions.correction: Substitute two different values into one equation and show that only one keeps the sides equal.

real_world_applications.example: Working out how many tickets a fixed budget will buy asks which number makes the cost match exactly.

pedagogy_recommendations.why_effective: Letting learners try values until the two sides agree makes the meaning of a solution self-evident.

learning_objectives.objective: Determine whether a proposed value is a solution by comparing the two sides.

learning_outcomes.outcome: Tests a given value in an equation and states whether it is a solution of it.

assessment_blueprint.recommended_question: Explain in your own words what it means to say that a value is a solution of an equation.
Is x = 4 a solution of 3x - 5 = 7? Give the value of each side.

concept.definition: The two sides of an equation are taken to be balanced, so carrying out the same mathematical operation on both leaves that balance undisturbed.

knowledge_items.statement: Performing an identical operation on the LHS and the RHS keeps the equation true, and a chain of such steps yields the solution.

abilities.ability: Apply one operation to both sides
abilities.description: Add, subtract, multiply or divide both sides by the same thing and write down the resulting equation.

ability_refs: Apply one operation to both sides

competencies.statement: Reaches the value of the variable through a chain of steps that keep the two sides equal.
ability_refs: Apply one operation to both sides

misconceptions.misconception: One side may be changed on its own
misconceptions.statement: Learners perform an operation on whichever side looks awkward and leave the other side exactly as it was.
misconceptions.root_cause: Tidying one side is a more visible goal than preserving the equality between the two.
misconceptions.correction: Use a two pan balance and lift a weight off only one pan, so the tilt is immediate and obvious.

real_world_applications.example: Sharing a bill equally means the same adjustment must be made to every person's share.

pedagogy_recommendations.why_effective: Working a physical balance with weights turns each algebraic step into a visible physical move.

learning_objectives.objective: Apply the same operation to both sides of an equation and write the new equation.

learning_outcomes.outcome: Solves a simple linear equation through a sequence of balanced operations on both sides.

assessment_blueprint.recommended_question: Solve 2x - 3 = 7 by doing the same operation to both sides at every step.
Why must an operation be applied to both sides of an equation rather than to one of them?

concept.definition: For 2x - 3 = 7, substituting x = 5 gives an LHS of 7 which equals the RHS, while x = 10 gives 17 which does not, so a claimed solution can always be tested.

knowledge_items.statement: A claimed solution is confirmed by putting it into the LHS and comparing the resulting value with the RHS.

abilities.ability: Test a claimed solution by substitution
abilities.description: Evaluate the LHS at the proposed value and set the result against the RHS.

skills.skill: Verifying an answer rather than trusting it
ability_refs: Test a claimed solution by substitution

competencies.statement: Confirms an answer independently before reporting it as final.
ability_refs: Test a claimed solution by substitution
skill_refs: Verifying an answer rather than trusting it

misconceptions.statement: Learners repeat their own solving steps as a check and so repeat the very mistake they made.
misconceptions.root_cause: Checking is understood as doing the sum again rather than as testing the answer by a different route.
misconceptions.correction: Substitute the answer into the original equation, which follows a path the working never took.

real_world_applications.example: An engineer substitutes a computed value back into the design condition before signing the drawing off.

pedagogy_recommendations.why_effective: Testing a correct and an incorrect value on the same equation makes the power of the check obvious.

learning_objectives.objective: Check a proposed solution of 2x - 3 = 7 by evaluating both sides at that value.

learning_outcomes.outcome: Substitutes a value into an equation and reports whether the two sides come out equal.

assessment_blueprint.recommended_question: Show that x = 5 satisfies 2x - 3 = 7 while x = 10 does not.
Why is substituting into the original equation a better check than repeating your own working?

concept.definition: Subtracting the same term from both sides amounts to moving that term to the other side, so transposition is a shorthand for the balancing operation and not a separate rule.

knowledge_items.statement: Moving a term across the equality sign with its sign changed simply records the effect of adding or subtracting it on both sides.

abilities.description: Move a term to the other side of an equation and change its sign as the move requires.

skills.skill: Shortening a routine without losing its justification
ability_refs: Transpose a term correctly

competencies.statement: Uses a shortcut while remaining able to explain the balanced step that lies behind it.
ability_refs: Transpose a term correctly
skill_refs: Shortening a routine without losing its justification

misconceptions.misconception: Transposing is a rule about crossing over
misconceptions.statement: Learners recite that a term changes sign when it crosses the equality sign without knowing why it does.
misconceptions.root_cause: The shortcut is taught as a rule to memorise before the balancing step it abbreviates has been shown.
misconceptions.correction: Write the subtraction on both sides in full once, then show the shortcut produces the identical line.

real_world_applications.example: Equation solving software rearranges terms by exactly this rule when it isolates a variable.

pedagogy_recommendations.why_effective: Learners can rehearse the mechanical move beforehand and spend the lesson on why it is legitimate.

learning_objectives.objective: Transpose a term across the equality sign and name the balanced step it replaces.

learning_outcomes.outcome: Rewrites an equation by transposing a term and states the equivalent operation on both sides.

assessment_blueprint.recommended_question: Solve 3x + 4 = 19 by transposing, writing the balanced step that each transposition stands for.
Assertion: transposing is a separate rule. Reason: a term changes sign when it crosses the equality sign.

concept.definition: In 2x - 3 = x + 2 the expression on the left is 2x - 3 and on the right is x + 2, so both sides carry the variable, unlike the equations of earlier classes.

knowledge_items.statement: An equation may carry the variable in its LHS and its RHS alike, as 2x - 3 = x + 2 does, which earlier classes never met.

abilities.ability: Gather the variable terms on one side
abilities.description: Move the variable terms to one side and the constants to the other before solving.

skills.skill: Reorganising an equation before solving it

competencies.statement: Brings like terms together so a two sided equation becomes one with a bare number on one side.

skill_refs: Reorganising an equation before solving it

misconceptions.statement: Learners transpose the constants but leave a variable term stranded on the side where it started.
misconceptions.root_cause: Every earlier example carried a bare number on one side, so only numbers were ever moved across.
misconceptions.correction: Point out that x stands for a number too, so a term in x transposes exactly like a constant.

real_world_applications.example: Comparing two mobile tariffs that each charge per minute puts the unknown on both sides of the equation.

pedagogy_recommendations.why_effective: Two competing price plans give a natural reason for the variable to appear on both sides at once.

learning_objectives.objective: Rearrange 2x - 3 = x + 2 so that the variable terms stand on one side only.

learning_outcomes.outcome: Solves an equation carrying the variable on both sides and states the value found.

assessment_blueprint.recommended_question: Solve 2x - 3 = x + 2 and check the answer in both sides of the original equation.

concept.definition: Where both sides carry bracketed expressions, opening them first turns an awkward equation into one of the familiar form, so simplification comes before solving.

knowledge_items.statement: Brackets on either side are opened first so the equation takes the familiar form before any transposing is attempted.

abilities.ability: Expand bracketed terms on both sides
abilities.description: Multiply out every bracket on the LHS and the RHS, then collect the like terms.

misconceptions.misconception: Solve and expand at the same time
misconceptions.statement: Learners begin transposing terms while brackets are still unopened and lose track of the signs.

misconceptions.correction: Require the fully expanded equation to be written on a line of its own before any transposing.

misconceptions.misconception: The check may be skipped when confident
misconceptions.statement: Learners leave out the final verification whenever their working felt straightforward at the time.
misconceptions.root_cause: The check produces no new answer, so it feels like effort spent for nothing once a value is in hand.
misconceptions.correction: Mark a worked example where a sign slip is caught only by the final comparison of the two sides.

concept.definition: Problems about numbers, ages, perimeters and combinations of currency notes can all be settled with linear equations, and the method's value lies in how varied those applications are.

knowledge_items.statement: Number puzzles, age problems, perimeter questions and currency note combinations all reduce to a linear equation in one variable.

misconceptions.misconception: The unknown must be the thing asked for
misconceptions.statement: Learners always let the variable stand for the quantity the question asks about, even when another choice is far simpler.
misconceptions.root_cause: Word problem drills usually name the unknown for the learner, so choosing it is never actually practised.
misconceptions.correction: Solve one age problem twice with different choices of unknown and compare how hard each becomes.

real_world_applications.example: Settling a shared expense among contributors who each hand over a different number of notes is done this way.

pedagogy_recommendations.why_effective: Collecting real problems from home and turning each into an equation shows the breadth of the method.

learning_objectives.objective: Formulate a linear equation in one variable from a stated problem on ages or perimeters.

learning_outcomes.outcome: Writes an equation from a word problem, solves it and interprets the answer in context.

assessment_blueprint.recommended_question: A rectangle's perimeter and a relation between its sides are given. Form a linear equation and find the sides.
Write your own problem about currency notes whose solution needs a linear equation, then solve it.
